title: Welcome to Kemi Alemoru's guest edit
alt: A headshot of Kemi Alemoru dressed in a red two piece holding a silver handbag
author: Kemi Alemoru

sections.heading: Editor's letter
body: The inaugural issue of Worn, Whering's first digital and IRL zine, was shepherded by the former Head of Editorial Content at Glamour magazine (with work seen in gal-dem, Dazed, i-D, Vogue, GQ). Here she tells us what's inside.

sections.html: You know that feeling where you walk over a bridge in the centre of the capital (let’s say Waterloo) on an evening when the air is charged, and you drink in the city skyline – our filthy river, our mishmash of modern monuments contrasting with storied historical architecture, and its characters, and you just clock it for a second. London is incredible. You may get the same pang walking down Rye Lane or Dalston High Street when the light hits a beautiful hipster in a majestic way, and you’re struck in awe by the natural style and beauty of this metropolis. They, along with the fashion industry machine, make London a style capital.

sections.alt: An image of a model on the go, covered with a mixed media collage of fashion items

sections.html: Fashion, like London, is a cruel mistress at times, but her grit, her pace, and the constant influx of new hungry talent mean she’s never boring, with a resilient underground scene and juggernaut houses that influence style worldwide. While fashion contributes £62 billion to the UK economy, the creative heartbeat of this industry – its designers, stylists, writers, photographers, and models – is what makes it magical.

Speaking to former collaborators and people I am a fan of was such a joy for this issue. Whering is a record of your personal style and it helps you keep track of the clothes that inspire you. Together, we’ve taken that ethos and brought readers behind the scenes of the season and, hopefully, given you inspiration to curate your own unique, storied closet via my favourite fashionistas. Whering’s first zine is a shrine to London fashion, from the POV of titans and those working their way up, insiders and those on its periphery.
Enjoy!

title: PRIYA AHLUWALIA'S MOODBOARD
alt: People in clothing face one another with arms extended near the sea, creating a dramatic, solemn scene under a dusky sky.
author: Kemi Alemoru

sections.heading: Founder of the multi-award-winning label Ahluwalia, Priya, gives us a peek into their moodboard.
body: One of the brightest names to return to the runway this season will be Priya Ahluwalia. Influenced by a kaleidoscope of cultures and histories from her upbringing in South London and her Nigerian-Indian heritage, her eco-conscious styles have been seen on the likes of Aimee Lou Wood for her Met Gala debut inspired by Congo Sapeurs; she created a custom look for Wumni Mosaku’s historic BAFTA win and counts Keke Palmer as a fan. But what is the 33-year-old’s collection evoking?

sections.html: Talk us through the moodboard you had in mind for your show.

It’s definitely a shift for us. There’s gonna be some staples from Ahluwahlia, but we’ve been experimenting with new silhouettes, and some of it’s more pared back than you’re used to seeing from me. I was thinking about how humans resist things politically through joy and community. On the mood board, there’s quite a lot of Kerry James Marshall artwork; there’s quite a lot of imagery of the Black Panthers. I kept finding Indian sculpture, and when I read the sculptors’ descriptions, it was all about emotional rebellion. There’s also rave culture because I’ve always found that people coming together and raving feels like a sign of resistance. I’m quite a research-heavy designer, but it’s never so referential that it becomes costumey. I like to subvert all the research. So even though that’s what’s on the board, it might not necessarily be immediately obvious when you see the collection.

sections.alt: albert howard hield lezing over black panther beweging
black panther newton seale congress assembly peace and freedom
sreekumar pillai

sections.html: Do you feel like resistance is a timely theme for what we’re going through right now?

Absolutely. I mean, God, I can’t think of much else. And to be honest with you, I’m not saying I’m changing the world with this collection, but I think even on a personal level, to look at these subjects and to explore them partly helps me process it, as well as doing all the other things I need to do to actually make change.

body: Five independent designers to pay attention to this fashion week.

sections.label: Video of man talking through five different indie designers to look out for

sections.html: Sharkkini

Initially known for its trompe l’oeil string vest t-shirts, they’ve just put out a brand new run which features everything from two-way coloured basketball shorts, amazing bikini sets, little hot pants, polo shirt dresses. References 90s and 00s streetwear, video vixens from R&B and rap videos. Described as the “effortlessly sensual uniform for the modern creative woman”.
Eden Tan

His masters collection a couple of years ago drew a lot of attention. He made a lot of incredible one-off pieces that were made on bolts of fabric, but he's also an amazing upcycler and has a really incredible range of upcycled rucksacks that are made out of motorbike jackets and incredible handbags that are upcycled from old pairs of high-heeled shoes that have this kind of Tom Ford-for-Gucci sort of sexiness and severity.

Now, you've probably seen some of the sexiest people that you know on Instagram wearing an F+ vest over the summer. It’s still a relatively new brand, but it has really exciting things coming up that you need to stay tuned for. Follow them on Instagram for more.
Ellie Misner

This is a designer who is making really high quality demi-couture dresses for a raft of amazing celebrity clients including Maisie Williams, Tyla, Halle Bailey, Rowan Blanchard, Jorja Smith and more. The overall look is these sumptuous incredible curves on beautiful ornate fabrics. Golds and champagnes and plums that are rendered in these beautiful stripes and tailored in the most pristine way so that the body's curves are really accentuated.
4FSB

4FSB (For Fuck’s Sake Babes) is designed by Jamie Bull and it’s an incredible selection of one of one caps and amazing t-shirts that have some of the most dark, sick graphics on the front. A little bit Aphex Twin “Windowlicker” vibes. They’re spooky, they’re funny, they’re perverse. It’s the perfect Halloween t-shirt.

title: ELLIE MISNER'S MOODBOARD
alt: Fashion model poses confidently in a vintage-inspired burgundy and striped corset dress, holding draped fabric against a softly lit studio backdrop.
author: Kemi Alemoru

sections.heading: A look into the mind and inspiration behind independent demi-couture label Founder Ellie Misner.
body: Ellie Misner’s East London-based eponymous couture label was recently seen on Maisie Williams on the red carpet for Practical Magic 2 but has been an it-girl favourite for those in the know since it started in 2022. The zero-waste corsetier has dressed Shygirl, Paloma Elsesser, Dove Cameron and SZA and takes inspiration from women’s bodies and memories. Her last collection, “It’s My Birthday, I Can Cry If I Want To,” explores the complex emotions of turning 30. What else is on her moodboard?

sections.html: What part of history or culture gets your juices flowing when you’re trying to think of your new creations?

Every collection has been based around myself, or a person in my life that I want to bottle the feeling of. Both my grandmas have passed away, but both of their houses had over-the-top art. Art Deco fixtures, sketches all over the walls. There were all these Japanese silk prints from Hong Kong, Venetian masks on the walls. My other grandma had amazing lamps, kind of like chachkis, or really ornate vintage perfume bottles. As a little kid, I was obsessed with it. A lot of my collections are quite inspired by those pieces because they’re in my studio now. I’m such a hoarder. Then I feel like these items mix with my love of shape and accentuating the curve of your body. My favourite is a recent striped dress with a big bow on the side; it’s very me.

sections.alt: Eclectic, elegant corner with two ornate table lamps, stacked art books on a glass table, gilded mirror, white curtains, and plants.
sections.caption: Courtesy of Ellie Misner

sections.alt: Three black-framed Art Deco fashion illustrations hang vertically beside a bright window and white curtain, creating an elegant vintage display.
sections.caption: Courtesy of Ellie Misner

sections.alt: Cluttered bookstore display piled with fashion books and magazines, brass tea sets, bronze figures, and a bright red Chinese ornament.
sections.caption: Courtesy of Ellie Misner

sections.html: Why are you not showing this fashion week?

London’s broke. London’s also stingy as f*ck. No one wants to part with their money. We also don’t have as much disposable income as the US as a fashion city. Unless I’m doing a lot of custom pieces for red carpet – I’ll get a call two days before a Tems event for a heart attack custom. I also love working with Raye and with Jorja Smith.

sections.heading: Confessions from the second row
body: Fashion certainly has a hierarchy, and it can be unglamorous work plotting your ascent while always making it look like you aren’t trying at all. One anonymous insider reports from the peripheries.

sections.html: After years of active duty on the front lines, sitting through countless fashion shows around the globe, I’ve earned my doctorate for conducting an anthropological study on the complex character that is the fashion devotee. Call me (a chic) David Attenborough.

Found basking in its natural habitat at fashion week, you’ll spot one in February and September making its biannual pilgrimage. In pursuit of fashionistas, I find myself aimlessly wandering around Zone 6 in a carefully curated outfit destined for the FROW. While dressed up like a turkey at Christmas, I spot a majestic peacock in the distance. Uncomfortably outside of its usual environment – this must be the place.

The invite said the show starts at 2pm, which in fashion terms could mean anything between 2pm and 3pm. 3:30 if it’s Mowalola. Timing this perfectly is an art I’ve sadly still not mastered. A minute too late and you’ll find yourself unsuccessfully bargaining with stony-faced security or a stubborn PR to let you in, protesting that you are invited, unlike the ticketless hordes hanging around nearby. Instead, I arrive fashionably early and accept the booby prize: Balancing painful small talk that rarely goes beyond how busy both of you are or bone-gnawing silence.

Outside the venue, a pride of peacocks strut up and down, desperately hoping to be candidly papped. Spotting the same faces outside (read: not inside) each and every season, I wonder what some of them actually do before remembering myself similarly camped outside Somerset House as a shameless fashion student.

I’m now deemed important enough to warrant a seat – more so as [insert middle management title] of [insert magazine title here] than in my own right – but, hey, no complaints. OK, well, a couple. Namely, a seat on the second row? Somewhere behind the fashion editor darling of the minute and the person who only acknowledges you in an empty room.

Entering the showspace – a cavernous, concrete structure that is ordinarily an underground car park – I sidle into my assigned seat on the shared bench past pouffes of tulle and a woman with JW Anderson’s pigeon-shaped purse. The bench groans, or maybe it’s just my fellow show-goers, irritated that yet another grifter has wormed their way into the second row from the shunned standing section. The irony? Our view is obscured by the FROW anyway, either by a comically large hat or Suzy Menkes’ signature pompadour.

It’s 2:22, and the show is starting – hallelujah it’s early! As the models whizz past in a blur to a thumping soundtrack, my second-row sisters struggle to capture content that feigns FROW status. Across the catwalk I spy a “serious” journalist from the Independent (or maybe he’s at Vogue.com now) furiously scribbling in a tiny notebook. I’m sure it’s either the words ‘denim’, ‘80s’ and ‘pastiche’ or a cry for help. Can I borrow the pen?

Quicker than it started, the show ends, and the stampede for the exit arrives. As the chaotic conga line crams out of a single tiny door, I wonder if this is the show I’ll get trampled to death leaving. Around me, the half-baked reviews rush in – ‘loved it!’ ‘Hated it!’ – and I remember this is only the first of eight shows today.
A million girls would kill for this job; yet here I am bitching about being stuck on a ladder that I have repeatedly and voluntarily chosen to climb. The only way is up!

title: NORDIC POETRY'S MOODBOARD
alt: Two fashion models pose in avant-garde black bodysuits, patterned tights, platform heels, and dramatic hairstyles against a pale blue backdrop.
author: Kemi Alemoru

sections.heading: We speak to Ameli Lindgren, Founder of the celebrity cult-following vintage archive Nordic Poetry.
body: Since opening in 2007, Nordic Poetry has become a fashion mecca for Gabriette, Charli XCX, Lily Allen, and Law Roach, who pose against the East London store’s nowviral pink walls. Ameli, an archive-design fanatic, even sourced Pink Pantheress’ cool-Britannia Vivienne Westwood gown for the Grammys. She tells us how she developed her curatorial eye.

sections.html: What are you a magpie for? What draws you in when looking for your pieces?

I was a 90s kid – I was born in the 70s but young in the 90s – and there’s a reason why people really want to wear that stuff. It was expressing freedom, which doesn’t happen as much as it used to. It’s a shame he’s made stupid mistakes because John Galliano is one of my favourite designers along with Vivienne Westwood and Alexander McQueen. They’re all British. I’m not from London. I’m Swedish. I moved to London because it was raw. I used to think Paris was very streamlined, and I still think it is in many ways, but London has that edge. I go back, and I find things that are wearable and fashionable but creative and fun.

sections.alt: Close-up of a person with an open mouth, white sunglasses, and layered gold chains spelling “SEX,” creating a bold, glamorous fashion mood.
sections.caption: Image courtesy of Ameli Lindgren

sections.alt: Two fashion models pose in avant-garde black bodysuits, patterned tights, platform heels, and dramatic hairstyles against a pale blue backdrop.
sections.caption: Image courtesy of Ameli Lindgren

sections.html: Are there any celebrities you’ve not yet encountered who you’d love to lend to?

We have such a huge clientele. We dress the biggest celebrities all around the world. I’m not a person who gets starstruck. That’s not why I started this. It’s for anyone to be able to wear something that resonates with them, that is unique, that has got a story. Also, I think everyone within the industry needs to be paid for what they do. We do very rare pieces. It’s taken a lot of time and effort. I started from nothing, and I’ve built an archive by myself through hard work. So no, we don’t lend for free.

title: PARTY GIRL'S GUIDE TO FW AFTERS
alt: The professional party girl’s guide to the catwalks after dark
author: Bee Beardsworth

sections.heading: The professional party girl’s guide to the catwalks after dark.
body: Bee Beardsworth speaks with Mahoro Seward, British Vogue Editor, Jack Guinness, Emma Winder, Mina Galán and Miss Jason on fashion parties.

sections.html: Ever since I was a little girl, I knew I wanted to be on the guest list. Alongside my longstanding fellowship with the Fashion Girl Society is a lifetime membership of the Party Girl Association. The party pages of my favourite glossies showed me a world of nocturnal soirées, documented in flashbulb photos. I imagined what it would be like to actually be one of the Party People – an attendee at a party so exclusive, rubbing shoulders with the talent and faces defining the zeitgeist, sipping champagne while looking like a supermodel and making the sort of iconic small talk Andy Warhol documented in his diaries.

Nearly a decade later, I’ve been to more fashion week parties than I can recall. This isn’t simply because of some ungodly level of intoxication – every fashion week, multiple nights back to back are stacked with more parties than seem possible, with countless brands trying to tap into that nighttime magic.

sections.text: "My personal record is four parties in one evening, with the last ending at 5am, followed by a quick power nap before attending a 9am show, makeup still on. They don’t call me a professional party girl for nothing."

sections.html: But what does it take to make it behind the rope, past the clipboard-wielding PR and into the hallowed halls of a properly glamorous, star-studded LFW soirée? Let the pros tell you how. Set an intention for the night Let’s get one thing straight: fashion week parties are usually less about dancing or outright fun and more about a dreaded third thing: networking. It’s the industry’s meeting point, a milieu of faces, names and roles. So, is there someone you want to meet, a brand you want to make yourself known to, or are you just there to rinse the free bar? Whatever it is, let your intention inform your actions. Or, as Mahoro Seward, British Vogue editor and LFW FROW royalty, puts it: “Being the person who turns up to every party is not chic, so pick what best serves you.” Pull a look This should be self-evident … it is fashion. Writer and lynchpin of the LFW scene Jack Guinness’s best advice is: “Whatever the brand gives you to wear.”

However, if you’ve not yet made it to the upper echelons of LFW status, “I used to dress a little more jazzy and camp. Now a black suit and boots seem to do the job. Glasses on if I’m feeling a little fruity.” Emma Winder, the internet’s favourite it girl, with a penchant for all things 70s and the dance moves to match, sticks to her staple idiosyncratic swag: “A vintage fitted suit and accessories that really do the talking.” My tip: dress like the centre of attention and you will become it. Guest list is a state of mind I may now be known on sight at every fête at LFW, but every true party girl first got her foot in the door based on the three Cs: cockiness, confidence and conviction.

sections.alt: Emma Winder - Fashion Week
sections.caption: Image courtesy of Emma Winder

sections.alt: Miss Jason - Fashion Week
sections.caption: Image courtesy of Miss Jason

sections.alt: Bee - Fashion Week
sections.caption: Image courtesy of Bee Beardsworth

sections.html: “My best tip is LIE,” says Jack. Mahoro seconds this: “Bulldoze your blag so hard that you convince the PR it’s a clerical error.” Mind your Ps and Qs When I moved to London, I didn’t know a single person. One thing I did know was how to say please and thank you. One victim of my charm is Max Harrison, aka Mayfair Max, doorman of infamy and the person to know if you want to get in anywhere that matters. “Be gracious, be patient, and don’t argue the toss,” he advises. “Know someone who is actually important inside if you’re going to try and be difficult. Sorry!” It’s a marathon, not a sprint Mahoro’s sage advice: “Hydration, electroly tes, and not starting on Martinis.”

“Don’t be the last one leaving the party,” Mina Galán, DJ, producer and fellow professional party girl, tells me, looking me in the eye and laughing. A classic example of do what we say, not what we do. Have fun. Recounting our favourite LFW memories, I narrow mine down to Harry Styles knocking over my cocktail years ago and bringing me a new one himself (those northern boys!), or lying in a bathtub of champagne in the Chiltern x Vogue party bathroom just months ago, wearing a lace-up SOSSKYN dress. Host, DJ and perennial it girl Miss Jason recalls a Nasir Mazhar party at Metropolis many moons ago with models, strippers and rappers. “It was like Sin City, and I leaned all the way in!”

sections.text: Dress like the centre of attention

sections.html: Jack recalls a night so iconic that all others pale in comparison. “I ended up disappearing with Lindsay Lohan and trying on Elizabeth Taylor’s coats and … well, I can’t say what happened next, but I think she covered most of it in her big Oprah interview.” And if none of the above works, one well-seasoned insider gave me a really cheeky tip. Find a willing friend, change their contact in your phone to the name of the exec PR in charge of the guest list, then fake texts and phone calls on the door to trick their foot soldiers. Where there is a will – and enough audacity – there is always a way.

title: HOW TO GET NOTICED AT FASHION WEEK
author: Anastasia Vartanian

sections.text: Dear Fat Anna Wintour… how do I get noticed at fashion week?

sections.html: Reader: What does it mean to be “noticed”? Do you want your Doechii moment, looking so fierce that the whole industry gasps: “behold, a new fashion icon!” This is what I pictured my first fashion week would go like. I soon realised no one actually cares that much. Plus celebrities have whole teams whose job it is to get them seen.

There’s different camps. Journalists who trek around shows all day and report back are stylish but sensible. Sneaker collabs with buzzy designers, carabiner skirts, vintage cardigans, designer caps, fluffy coats and oversized sunglasses. Items which signal your superior sartorial knowledge without being too cumbersome.

Influencers and celebrities look more exciting (and impractical). If I get stares on the tube en route, it’s a pretty good sign that my look will get some attention. Giant platforms and bulbous garments guarantee a street style snap, but they make travelling from show to show quite hellish. Especially if you don’t have a Zone 1 hotel or a personal driver, luxuries reserved for the most high-profile talent and publications. A crazy look ≠ being noticed. Perhaps you have a signature, like Beka Gvishiani of StyleNotCom’s blue cap.

Networking beforehand is much more exciting. The easiest way to get photographed at a show is to wear the brand in question. Designers often lend out clothes to attendees; it’s worth asking! PR showrooms also lend garments for events to get press for their designers. Also, do you have friends in fashion? Make-up or hair artists, stylists, designers? Work with them! They might push you out of your comfort zone.

If you plan to go all out with your look, focus your efforts on one or two events a day – doing a quick change when necessary. Last season, drag queen Krystal Versace shared how she wriggled in and out of outfits in her taxi between shows. I got changed in a Five Guys toilet.

Don’t forget: You can stand out by just being a genuine person. In these rooms, there are people who stare through you if you don’t have the right follower count or job title. Take the time to actually connect: a couple of great conversations are much better than 20 surface-level ones. IRL interactions matter as much as getting a good photo for your socials. You may not get a job offer immediately, but every fashion week will add collaborators, colleagues, and comrades.

title: FW: PHOTOGRAPHERS POV
alt: Street style photography at Fashion Week
author: Anna Cafolla

sections.heading: Anna Cafolla, American Vogue's News Editor, speaks with Street Style Photographer Noorunisa & Vogue Scandinavia Columnist Verona Farrell (@secondhandhuns).
body: What the street style photographers really think of you.
At any fashion week, there are the people going to the shows, the people trying to look like they’re going to the shows, and the photographers who can tell the difference.

sections.html: British-Pakistani photographer Noorunisa has lensed the fitted-out arrivals of London, Paris, Milan and New York, as well as fashion’s increasingly influential Copenhagen circuit. Outside Marni in Paris, she has caught Usher without his usual security circle, Erykah Badu in full flamboyant flight, and footballer Achraf Hakimi. But the people with invitations are only half the story.

“A crazy increase in people standing outside of shows who aren’t actually attending,” is one of fashion month’s biggest shifts, she says. There are aspiring influencers, celebrity fans, and bewildered tourists. “Fans come with signs, balloons, and ladders. Trying to do your job around all of that is seriously taxing.” The circus has become sentient. “People are so aware of how they’re perceived, who the photographers are, and who we shoot for,” says Noorunisa. “I’ve heard of people asking to know which photographers to look out for or befriend just so they can have a chance of being published somewhere.” (Other times, you’ll find yourself stonewalled by a gaggle of models outside a Victoria Beckham show.)

sections.html: “In the beginning, street style felt much more accidental,” agrees Acielle, a Belgium-based photographer; if Vogue is your Fashion Month nucleus, it’s Acielle’s visuals you’re poring over. “People were simply going to shows, and photographers started noticing the interesting characters around them.” On the first morning of a Big Four fashion week, Acielle’s inner monologue is less ‘Who is that?’ than logistical whirring. “My first thought is: Where is the light? You’re watching clothes, people, movement, light, backgrounds, and the energy of the crowd all at once.”

Paris remains her “gold standard,” precisely because it “balances highfashion polish with eccentric personal style.” But in an age of algorithmic fashion and trends consuming trends, polish isn’t enough. “I’ve always enjoyed photographing those moments when fashion is still experimental and slightly undefined. I don’t really look for trends. I’m more interested in surprises.” Sometimes, though, you’re watching a trend transmutate in front of you. Dublin born, Stockholmbased creator and writer Verona Farrell, better known as @secondhandhuns, remembers clocking people wearing flip-flops in Copenhagen in 2020, “for the first time outside of the context of the beach.” She had only just started shooting street style. “I felt like I was acting as a messenger of the trend—the Danes are so creative in how they style functional clothing.”

couldn’t let a good outfit go”.

sections.html: For the next three years, she could barely switch off. “I could have been having a super serious conversation and I would start running after strangers—I couldn’t let a good outfit go.” Farrell’s preference for iPhone video made her an outlier at first, before her style of shooting became ubiquitous. “People started repeating my format, copying my text and sounds, and everything I developed as a series…and weren’t doing it very well!”

Acielle’s work compels her to seek out individuality: “I’ve seen every possible trend come and go. The people who are most memorable are usually the ones who have found a way to make fashion feel like their own. Personal style is a form of storytelling.” It’s in New York, Farrell says, that she meets a different species of street style subject altogether. “People are ready to be seen and perform.” And after years spent studying exactly how people dress when they know— or desperately hope—a camera is watching, the photographers themselves are not immune.

After one particularly outré Paris Fashion Week, Noorunisa went home and bleached her eyebrows. “I think I had an identity crisis!” she says. She’s since learned restraint, but aside from perilous weather conditions and some calculated would-be subjects, the sudden urge to reach for the bleach might be the main occupational hazard of making everyone else feel seen.

title: YOMI ADEGOKE: INSIDE THE CLOSET
alt: A woman in a black top and pink patterned skirt sits among folded clothes, with shelves of colourful shoes behind her.
author: Kemi Alemoru

sections.heading: We caught up with Elle contributing editor, Guardian columnist and bestselling author of The List, Yomi Adegoke for her LFW edit.
body: If you’re as nosy as I am, you might also wonder how fashion’s front row always manages to look so well put together. Well, Whering decided that, in the run-up to Fashion Week, we would raid their real-life closets to get their edit of go-to looks for when you want to be ready for your close-up.

sections.html: “I love taking risks. Since I was younger, I’ve loved icebreaking, conversation-starting pieces. I love walking around with logomania bags because people just assume that it’s fake, so I never get robbed. But I also don’t like feeling like I’m walking around in costume, so I will mix the out-there pieces with something a bit more pared back. I love mixing references.

I love art and music, and I do think fashion is now an extension of that expression. I think when I had long hair it read as cutesy. Now I have no hair; it reads as catwalk. I definitely have got more bonkers as time has gone on, though. My Charles Jeffrey shoes, which I got at a sample sale for £100 down from £1500, are in my top five in my shoe collection.

sections.text: “I’ve landed on quite a man-repellent style”

sections.html: The claws really love to fall out, but I found the one cobbler on the planet that could replace them. They kind of are a weapon, but a very chic one. Fashion week is a time for a lot of experimentation, and whereas before I would want to look cute – everyone looks sexy, you’re going to all these parties, you never know who you’re gonna meet – I’ve landed on quite a man-repellent style.

I’m in my mid-30s, so f*ckability isn’t really very high on my list of things I’m even thinking about when it comes to dressing. The other day I was wearing this gorgeous piece by Dye Lab, the Nigerian brand. It’s a modern twist on the agbada, which is a type of traditional dress, and I was wearing it, and I looked in the mirror, and I was like, ‘Oh my god! Like, I literally look like a floating blob.’”

title: NANA ACHEAMPONG: INSIDE THE CLOSET
alt: Smiling woman in a red top sits in a zebra-print chair amid colourful clothing racks, wearing layered beads and earrings; joyful mood.
author: Kemi Alemoru

sections.heading: A behind-the-scenes look at Fashion Broadcaster and Editor at SheerLuxe Nana Acheampong's wardrobe.
body: Our resident editor, Kemi Alemoru, Former Head of editorial at Glamour UK goes into the closet with Nana.

sections.html: “It’s so cliché, but fashion should be fun. I really pride myself on being the most overdressed person in the room. Maybe I belong to the peacocking camp. Who knows? I love colour, I love print, I love texture, so my outfit is always going to be based around one of those aspects.

The items I love the most when it comes to my wardrobe are my shoes. I have to start off with an amazing pair of heels. They are the basis for me for any good outfit. I don’t own any flat shoes unless they are for the gym, so my heels are definitely my prized possession. I am of the camp that believes a lot of your clothes or a lot of your wardrobe should be seasonless.

sections.alt: A collage of close up shots of Nana Acheampong and her favourite wardrobe items

sections.html: I’m such a Spring/Summer girly that I adapt all those items for winter by adding a layer and a pair of boots, and I never put away my summer clothes. They are out year-round, and I will find a way to wear them in winter. I’m not going to go out in a strapless dress if it’s snowing. But yeah, other than that, most items work in all seasons.
